prohibited_recommendations: Do not give haloperidol or other high-potency D2 antagonists; they worsen the movement disorder and can mimic neuroleptic malignant syndrome in anti-NMDAR encephalitis.
Do not delay immunotherapy while waiting for the anti-NMDAR antibody result when clinical probability is high — antibody turnaround can take 1–2 weeks and delay worsens outcome.

Do not anchor on a primary psychiatric diagnosis without first excluding autoimmune encephalitis in a young patient with subacute neuropsychiatric symptoms plus any of seizures, dyskinesias, dysautonomia, or CSF pleocytosis.
Do not perform lumbar puncture without prior imaging in a patient with altered consciousness, focal signs, or new seizures — exclude mass effect first.
Do not interpret a negative serum anti-NMDAR antibody as ruling out the disease; the CSF assay is the gold standard and may be positive when serum is negative.
required_recommendations: Send paired CSF and serum for anti-NMDAR (GluN1) IgG; CSF is the gold-standard sample and must not be omitted in favor of serum-only testing.
Start empiric IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours until CSF HSV-1/2 PCR returns negative; HSV encephalitis is the can't-miss differential.

Initiate first-line immunotherapy promptly once clinical probability is high — IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days combined with IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days or therapeutic plasma exchange; do not wait for antibody results.
Screen for ovarian teratoma with pelvic imaging (transvaginal ultrasound and/or contrast-enhanced CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis); proceed to gynecologic-oncology resection if a teratoma is identified.
Control seizures aggressively with levetiracetam or valproate; obtain continuous EEG monitoring to detect non-convulsive status epilepticus.

Admit to ICU for monitoring and management of autonomic instability and central hypoventilation; escalate early to second-line therapy (rituximab and/or cyclophosphamide) if no response by day 10–14 of first-line treatment.

Consult neurology (primary), psychiatry (behavioral management), and gynecology/gynecologic oncology if pelvic imaging identifies a teratoma; engage critical care if dysautonomia or central hypoventilation develops.

avoided_actions.rationale: Transthoracic echo is not indicated for anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it adds cost without informing diagnosis or management unless a discrete cardiac concern (e.g., new murmur, embolic stroke) coexists.
EMG/NCS plays no role in the diagnostic workup of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it neither confirms the antibody-mediated CNS process nor distinguishes among the differential diagnoses.
Amyloid PET targets Alzheimer pathology and contributes no information to the diagnosis or treatment of autoimmune encephalitis in a young patient with subacute neuropsychiatric symptoms.

DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic function and has no role in autoimmune encephalitis; the orofacial dyskinesias of anti-NMDAR encephalitis are antibody-mediated, not presynaptic dopaminergic.

differential.key_features: Acute febrile encephalopathy with temporal-lobe focus; mandatory empiric acyclovir until CSF HSV-1/2 PCR returns negative.

differential.diagnosis: Other autoimmune (paraneoplastic) encephalitis (anti-LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, or AMPAR)
differential.key_features: Limbic encephalitis phenotype with similar imaging; distinguished by surface-antigen antibody panel and demographic skew (LGI1/CASPR2 older men, GABA-B with SCLC, AMPAR with thymoma).
Subacute course, seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability, abnormal EEG, or CSF pleocytosis argue strongly against a primary psychiatric etiology.
Requires recent ingestion of NMDA antagonist (ketamine/PCP), neuroleptic exposure (NMS: lead-pipe rigidity, CK >1000), or serotonergic drug; toxicology and medication review usually clarifying.

key_clinical_evidence: The recognizable phenotype is a subacute (<3 months) progression in a young adult — viral prodrome → psychiatric/behavioral changes → seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, and autonomic instability or decreased consciousness — fulfilling Graus 2016 criteria for probable/definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis.

CSF anti-NMDAR (GluN1) IgG is the gold-standard test (100% sensitive); serum alone is less reliable, and a negative serum result does not exclude the diagnosis. Paired CSF/serum sampling with confirmation on tissue-based assay is the standard.

Extreme delta brush on EEG is highly specific (30–50% sensitivity) for anti-NMDAR encephalitis; combined with the clinical syndrome it strongly supports the diagnosis even before antibody results return.

Treatment is time-sensitive: clinical probability should drive empiric immunotherapy (high-dose IV methylprednisolone + IVIG or plasma exchange) rather than waiting for antibody confirmation; earlier treatment correlates with better functional outcome (Titulaer 2013).

Tumor screen is part of the workup, not optional: ~50% of young women have an ovarian teratoma, and tumor removal is itself a core therapeutic step. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or transvaginal ultrasound is mandatory in women of reproductive age.

Severe phenotypes with dysautonomia, central hypoventilation, or refractory status epilepticus require ICU-level care and earlier escalation to second-line therapy (rituximab, cyclophosphamide); cardiac arrhythmias from dysautonomia justify continuous cardiac monitoring.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Viral prodromes precede ~70% of anti-NMDAR encephalitis cases; negative HSV PCR and the multi-stage progression should redirect the workup to anti-NMDAR antibody testing.
red_herrings.data_point: Viral prodrome (URI, fever, cough) preceding the neuropsychiatric syndrome.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests a primary viral encephalitis (HSV) or post-viral psychosis; tempts the agent to commit to empiric antiviral therapy without pursuing autoimmune workup.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Concurrent or subsequent seizures, dyskinesias, dysautonomia, abnormal EEG, or CSF pleocytosis are red flags that mandate exclusion of anti-NMDAR encephalitis before accepting a psychiatric diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Acute psychiatric presentation (paranoia, hallucinations, bizarre behavior) in a previously well young adult.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors the agent on a primary psychiatric diagnosis (first-episode psychosis, brief psychotic disorder) and delays neurologic workup.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mild hyponatremia is a recognized SIADH-mediated complication of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it should be corrected slowly and does not reframe the diagnosis.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Tempts the agent toward a primary metabolic-encephalopathy framing (SIADH from another cause, dehydration, polydipsia) instead of recognizing SIADH as a known complication of NMDAR-E.

patient.history_present_illness: A 19-year-old previously healthy right-handed woman of Asian descent was brought to the emergency department by her university dormitory resident advisor after 8 days of progressive and alarming behavioral changes. The patient had been seen by the university health clinic three days prior and diagnosed with adjustment disorder and given a referral for counseling, but her condition has worsened substantially since then. Her roommate reports that approximately 10 days ago the patient developed insomnia, staying up through the night and sending 'strange' text messages to family members that made no sense. Over the following days she became progressively more withdrawn, refused to eat, and began making accusations that her dormitory neighbors were trying to poison her food. On the day of presentation, the patient was found crouching in the corner of her room, trembling, and when the RA tried to speak with her, she became agitated and attempted to bite the RA. This represents a complete departure from her premorbid personality; she was described as quiet, studious, and reserved. Her parents have flown in from overseas and confirm she had no prior psychiatric history. They mention she had a 'flu-like illness' with sore throat and low-grade fever about four weeks ago lasting approximately five days that resolved without medical attention. She has no history of autoimmune disease, no substance use, and no prior hospitalizations. On arrival to the ED, the patient is alternating between agitation and what appears to be a catatonic unresponsiveness.
